Hi friends 👋,
Stocks are worth $0 now (I think, haven’t checked) and the string of perfect weather in NYC has ended, but the optimism streak continues! The world’s researchers and engineers are still cooking up the good stuff, and we’re here to serve it to you.
Let’s get to it.
Runway is building foundational AI for how the world creates. 65M+ people use Runway to generate, edit and produce video, images and audio with 80+ top media models. You can read my essay with co-founder Anastasis Germanidis to learn more on where Runway is headed beyond video.
Nvidia, Amazon, Lionsgate, Chime, and 95%+ of the Fortune 100 are part of a growing community of teams, founders, and independent creators using Runway to make national TV spots, social ads at scale, launch videos and more.
You can also use Runway in ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Cursor, Replit and more via the Runway MCP.
FDA / INOVIO, video by Runway
Last Friday, just a few hours after I hit send on the Dose, the FDA granted accelerated approval to INOVIO’s Voceryq, the first plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy approved in the US.
Voceryq will be used to treat recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, a disease I’d never heard of but sounds awful. Caused by HPV types 6 and 11, RPP gives victims wart-like growths in the airway, usually around the vocal cords, that make their voices hoarse, make them cough, and in severe cases, make it hard to breathe.
Surgeons can remove the growths, but the virus remains in the tissue, so the throat growths keep coming back, and patients end up in the operating room again and again for years. In the trial, 26 adults had needed at least three surgeries in the year before treatment.
As shown in the video above, Voceryq delivers two plasmids (small loops of DNA originally borrowed from bacteria) into muscle cells. One carries instructions for HPV-6 and HPV-11 proteins, which teaches the immune system to go after infected cells, and the other carries IL-12, a molecule that turns the immune response up. A device fires brief electrical pulses that open temporary pores in cell membranes so the DNA can get inside without requiring a virus for delivery.
After treatment, 7 of the 26 patients in the trial didn’t need surgery for the entire following year. It’s a small open-label trial, and INOVIO still has to confirm the results in a follow-up study, but it’s on the path now, which thank god, because this was the last shot. The company was set to run out of cash in Q1 2027, but its stock tripled in after hours after posting the results.
This isn’t the first treatment for RPP - Precigen’s Papzimeos, which uses a modified virus to target the same HPV types, won full approval in August 2025.
RPP patients have gone from no treatments beside surgery to two, which is amazing, but the platform will likely prove to be even more important.
If you can get a plasmid into cells and get the immune system to act on it, you can swap in instructions for other HPV diseases, cancers, and infections, which is what INOVIO is planning to do next.
DN-AYYYYYY!
There are very few companies out there as cool as Zipline. After starting by serving hospitals and health facilities across Africa, where they were allowed to fly drones and the need was most acute, they came to America last year to do deliveries, starting in Texas.
CEO Keller Clifton said that over the past 18 months, they’ve grown flight volumes 18x and are now doing more that a million deliveries per year per metro.
Now, they’re going to be able to do a lot more. The company raised $1.5 billion at a $21.5 billion valuation in a round led by Paradigm, WCM, and Layer.
They’re using the money to bring drone deliveries nationwide. To that end, they signed “the largest autonomous vehicle contract in human history to expand automated delivery nationally with Walmart,” with whom they’ll scale to 300 supercenters throughout these United States.
This is awesome news. Zipline’s drones are quiet, safe (they’ve done over 150M commercial autonomous miles with no safety incidents), fast, affordable, and don’t require a human chaperone. As I wrote in my Deep Dive on Airbound, I’m incredibly optimistic that a good deal of movement will move to the skies, and this is an important step in that direction.
Since the Eagles stink and I can’t use this on them much, I’ll use it here:
Fly Zipline Fly.
In April, Owl Posting wrote an essay on “new knobs of control,” including DREADDS, which he explains like this:
You use a viral vector to deliver the DREADD gene to whatever cells you want to control. Once the DREADD is expressed on the cell surface, it just sits there, inert. Then you administer CNO, which binds exclusively to the DREADDs. When it binds, the receptor activates its coupled G-protein just like any normal GPCR would, doing whatever you engineered the GPCR to do. And, as far as anyone can tell, there are no off-target effects.
This is unambiguously a new knob. The receptor didn’t exist in your body before. Its binding partner (CNO) doesn’t exist endogenously. As a result, you, and you alone, get to decide when and where it is turned on.
Well, now we have them. In the first adult human study, per a Grok explainer in the replies, “doctors placed inhibitory DREADDs in the hippocampus of 3 people with medication-resistant epilepsy. Taking the drug quieted the seizure-causing cells, cutting seizures by ~93% with only mild side effects. It lets doctors precisely dial down overactive brain circuits on demand.”
That is wild. We have a knob that can turn down epilepsy.
DARPA
If we’re going to become a spacefaring civilization, we’re going to need to build bigger structures in space than can fit in a rocket. Today, there are two options for big space things: we can fold something up like origami and unfold it in orbit, which is how the James Webb Space Telescope works, or take the ISS approach, where you launch big pieces over many missions and put them together by hand.
Until now!
DARPA’s NOM4D program (Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials and Mass-efficient Design, great name) is working on a third option. They can send up a box of parts and assemble them in an automated way. On Thursday, DARPA announced that a Caltech payload had done just that, in what the agency calls the first-ever demonstration of automated in-space assembly. Hopefully, it’s the first of many many.
In this case, a simple gantry robot, which moves along three straight axes, joined composite truss pieces with custom connectors one section at a time while unrolling a thin reflective mesh. It is a proof of concept for future space antennas.
Program manager Andrew Detor compared the system to Tinkertoys or K’nex. It’s meant to be super simple, without fancy robotics or advanced algorithms. NOM4D is aiming at structures hundreds of meters to kilometers across, like space depots, habitats, huge solar arrays, and radio antennas large enough to listen all the way to the edges of the universe.
And speaking of making things in space, not boring capital portfolio company Varda is currently making drugs in space!
A couple of years ago, after listening to Season 1 of The Telepathy Tapes, I wrote The Return if Magic, and then I kept going down the rabbit hole, which led to pieces like Means & Meaning and Riding the Leopard.
Season 3 came out last month, and it’s on reincarnation. Reincarnation is a compelling bridge to believing that the world is more magical than we appreciate. For one thing, an awful lot of the world’s people believe in reincarnation as part of their religion, but for another, it’s a surprisingly well-researched topic. Since psychiatrist Ian Stevenson created the Division of Perceptual Studies (DOPS) at the University of Virginia in the 1960s, researchers there have documented and coded more than 2,500 cases worldwide of young children who spontaneously report detailed memories of previous lives.
I don’t want to spoil the series, but I do think you should give it a listen and consider what it might mean if it’s true.
With all the Means stories we cover here in the Dose, mix in a little Meaning.
And while we’re add it, this popped up in my feed yesterday…
Read more

A couple of years ago, after listening to Season 1 of The Telepathy Tapes, I wrote The Return if Magic, and then I kept going down the rabbit hole, which led to pieces like Means & Meaning and Riding the Leopard.

Since psychiatrist Ian Stevenson created the Division of Perceptual Studies (DOPS) at the University of Virginia in the 1960s, researchers there have documented and coded more than 2,500 cases worldwide of young children who spontaneously report detailed memories of previous lives.

Diabetes: In TRANSCEND-T2D-1, presented at ADA in June, 75–83% of patients got their A1C to 6.5% or lower in 40 weeks.

Knees: In TRIUMPH-1, knee osteoarthritis pain fell by about three-quarters.
Liver: In a Phase 2 substudy, 93% of patients on the top dose had normal liver fat after 48 weeks.
The drug hasn’t even hit the market yet (if you don’t count the grey market). Lilly, which crushed earnings this week and raised its full year revenue outlook by $5 billion, deserves every dollar of its $1.3T market cap.

This week’s news out of Neuralink is one of those.
ALS, or Lou Gehrig’s Disease, is a fatal, progressive neurodegenerative disorder that destroys the motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord that control voluntary muscle movement. It takes away its victims’ ability to speak even though it leaves their mind intact, meaning they can think clearly but can’t verbalize those thoughts.
Neuralink has been working to fix that with VOICE. Before VOICE, the best published result on the same vocabulary size, Stanford’s 2023 system, managed 62 words per minute with nearly a quarter of words wrong.
Natural conversation runs around 160 words per minute, so we’re about halfway there. Importantly, the system can also speak in the participant’s pre-ALS voice.
VOICE launched at UT Southwestern last October with FDA Breakthrough Device designation and plans to enroll up to six people with ALS, spinal cord injury, or stroke. That’s not a big group, and the one person in this study is just one-sixth of that. But every person who’s able to get their voice back through a BCI is a win, and the technology will only get better, faster, more accurate, and less invasive from here.
In related news, Elon Musk announced yesterday that its second product, Blindsight, which will restore sight to the blind, is ready engineering-wise.
Age of Miracles, pending regulatory approval.

We hate cancer here at the Dose, and we’re not afraid to say it. It’s probably why not a single cancer reads the Dose. We’re willing to sacrifice our numbers for our belief.
Consequently, we love when humans come up with new ways to kill cancer, and they’ve done it once again (and again, and again) this week.

On Monday, the FDA granted dostarlimab (GSK's Jemperli) accelerated approval as a standalone first treatment for stage II and III rectal cancers that are mismatch repair deficient (dMMR). These tumors basically have a broken DNA spell-checker, so mutations pile up until the cancer looks foreign to the immune system. Dostarlimab blocks PD-1, the off switch tumors use to keep T cells at bay, which lets the immune system clear the cancer (explained in the video above).

I got to see a preview of this at Onto Ventures’ summit in California a couple weeks ago and it was one of the most mindblowing demoes I’ve seen. Justin is kind of like the Lorax, but he speaks to the trees.
We cover a lot of impressive accomplishments in the Dose, like talking to plants and curing cancer, but it’s not every day that we cover a company that’s succeeded where the inimitable Sir Isaac Newton failed.
That’s what Marathon Fusion has done. Newton, under the pseudonym Jeova Sanctus Unus, spent three decades trying to crack alchemy, as I wrote about in Take Weird Ideas Seriously. I think it’s great that he tried. He just didn’t have the technology.
Marathon Fusion seems to. Fast neutrons from a deuterium-tritium fusion reaction knock a neutron out of mercury-198, which becomes mercury-197 and decays into gold over a few days.
Gold dropped pretty hard yesterday (unsure if related), but for now, it’s just a demonstration.

It’s a very Fuse-like bet that the neutrons produced in fusion reactions can be very valuable long before Q>whatever, and a Small Steps approach to fusion.
Or as Mike Meyers would say, “I LOVE GOOOOOOOOLD.”
